name: Lena Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Millbrook by half six. It's three thousand free-range hens, an apple orchard and some hay fields. First thing is walking the hen sheds, picking up floor eggs, checking for dead birds, then on the packing line. The grading machine weighs and sorts the eggs already, so I'm the one who catches cracked ones and fills the trays. Winter I'm out pruning apple trees with Rosa, and I'm still the worst pruner on the farm, she redoes half of mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you worked there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years. Before that it was twenty-five years at the supermarket, on the tills and then stacking shelves. They put in the self-checkouts, cut my hours to sixteen a week, and you can't live on sixteen. So I went to Millbrook. My husband Imran drives a delivery van, he's 53, five years younger than me. Between the two of us we earn just enough, and if the washing machine breaks we're in trouble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My daughter Sara put one on my phone. I use it to write a letter to the council or to ask what's wrong when a hen's got a pale comb. I check what it says with the farm manager, Mr Hale, though. It's handy, but I don't trust it the way Sara does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's like the self-checkouts. Lots of fuss, some jobs cut, then life goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overblown and leave it there. I'm not one to gloat or argue. At work we'd laugh about it over a cup of tea in the egg room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay hard but the same. Hard but the same I can manage, I've done it for years. I'd still worry about Imran's van, because they keep talking about vans without drivers, but that's a separate story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep learning the pruning so Rosa stops redoing mine. Try to put something by, even 10 a week, so the washing machine isn't a disaster. Maybe ask Mr Hale if I could learn to set up the grading machine, because then I'm more use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Tired, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the self-checkouts. How did that go for you at the supermarket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They told us it was to help us, to take the queues off. A year later they'd cut the till hours by half. Nobody was sacked, they just cut you down until you left by yourself. That's what I watch for now. Not the sacking, the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'hard but the same' look like in a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent on the 1st, Imran's van insurance on the 15th, and by the 25th we're eating whatever's in the freezer. Mr Hale lets us take the cracked eggs home, which helps more than you'd think. I make a lot of omelettes.

S0.say: I'd say it was overblown and leave it there, and laugh about it over tea in the egg room. I'm not one to gloat or argue.
S0.think: Things stay hard but the same, which I can manage. I'd still worry about my husband's delivery van, because people talk about vans without drivers.
S0.do: Keeps working and practises pruning so a colleague stops redoing her trees. Saves 10 a week for emergencies and asks the manager to teach her to set up the grading machine.
S0.quote: Nobody was sacked, they just cut you down until you left by yourself.
S0.fieldNote: Lena has already lived through automation at the supermarket, and the lesson she took is to watch hours, not sackings. Her household is tight to the day of the month. She also worries about her husband's delivery job, a second exposure in the same home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one that sounds like what actually happens. Bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard for some people, and that we need training for the ones who have to change, but I'd also say you can't stop progress. Both are true. I'd say that to the girls in the egg room and to my sister on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Millbrook would buy a machine to pack the trays, because that's the boring part and machines are good at boring. I'd lose hours, not my job, the way it went at the supermarket. And Imran's van might go the same way, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hale straight away what he's planning and if I can learn the new machines. I'd use the AI on my phone more, to learn what I can about how egg packers work. And I'd save harder, 20 a week if I can, and tell Imran to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I've been here before, so it's not a shock, just a weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose hours, not your job. How many hours could you lose before it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm on thirty-two now. At twenty-six we're short every month. At twenty I'd have to find something else, and there's nothing else, the care home and the petrol station, both full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the pruning, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a while, I think. Rosa says a robot can't see which branch to cut, you need to know the tree. But in a few years, who knows. I'd want to be good at pruning before then.

S1.say: I'd say it'll be hard for some and we need training for those who have to change, but you can't stop progress. Both are true.
S1.think: The farm would buy a machine to pack trays, and I'd lose hours rather than my job, as at the supermarket. My husband's van might go the same way.
S1.do: Asks the manager what he's planning and whether she can learn the new machines. Uses her phone's AI to learn how egg packers work and saves 20 a week, urging her husband to save too.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a weight she's carried before rather than a shock.
S1.quote: At twenty I'd have to find something else, and there's nothing else, the care home and the petrol station, both full.
S1.fieldNote: Lena talks in hours, not jobs: she knows exactly where her budget breaks, at about twenty-six hours a week. Her public line balances sympathy with acceptance of progress, which fits her centre views. She sees pruning as the skill to protect herself with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then it's both of us at once, me and Imran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government had better act fast, with money for people while things settle down. I don't normally want handouts, but if everyone's out at once, that's not a handout, it's an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the van and the hens in the same year. If they can do any job, Imran's van drives itself and the hen shed has a robot walking it. Two incomes gone, and I'm 60 and he's 55. I don't know how we'd keep the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Imran and cut everything, phones, the car insurance, presents. We'd talk about moving somewhere cheaper, maybe the flat above my sister's shop. I'd start making jam and chutney from the orchard windfalls to sell at the Saturday market, small money but real. And I'd ask the girls if they could help with rent for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't usually say that word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would be harder to say to your daughters, that you need money, or that you're moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money. Moving, they'd understand, people move. But I was the one who put Sara through college with the till money. Asking her for rent turns everything upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does only having two years' warning change things for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years you can't save, you can't learn a trade, you can only cut. We'd cut and hope. If it was ten years, I'd be retired before it came, but Imran wouldn't be, and two years catches us both at once.

S2.say: I'd say government must act fast with money for people while things settle down. If everyone's out at once, it's an emergency, not a handout.
S2.think: My husband's van and the hen shed could both go in the same year, so two incomes disappear while I'm 60 and he's 55. I don't know how we'd keep the flat.
S2.do: Cuts phones, insurance and presents with her husband and considers moving to the cheaper flat above her sister's shop. Sells jam and chutney from orchard windfalls at the Saturday market and asks her daughters for rent help.
S2.feel: Frightened, a word she doesn't usually use.
S2.quote: I was the one who put Sara through college with the till money. Asking her for rent turns everything upside down.
S2.fieldNote: For Lena, fast AGI is a household event: her income and her husband's could vanish together. She normally dislikes handouts but called this an emergency. Asking her daughter for rent hurts more than moving house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63, Imran 58. A bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, so let's plan: training for people like Imran, help for the older ones to get to their pension. I'd say it in a reasonable way, I'm not one for shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives us a few years to build a cushion and maybe get Imran into something safer. I'd have three years before my pension, which is hard but not impossible if Imran's still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the jam stall now, not later, and put every bit of it in savings. I'd use the AI on my phone more to learn things, like how to price the jam and what licence you need. And I'd push Imran to look at other work, maybe the council depot, before the vans change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I feel like I can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Imran to get him to think about other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, remember the self-checkouts. I waited too long at the supermarket, hoping it would turn round. Don't wait like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other farms' egg rooms. When I hear the Dobsons have no one on their packing line, I'll know it's next. I'd want our savings in place before then.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to plan: training for people like my husband and help for older workers to reach their pension. I'd say it reasonably.
S3.think: Five years gives us time to build a cushion and get my husband into safer work. Three years before my pension is hard but possible if he's still earning.
S3.do: Starts the jam stall now and saves everything it earns, using her phone's AI to learn pricing and licensing. Pushes her husband to look at work like the council depot before the vans change.
S3.quote: I waited too long at the supermarket, hoping it would turn round. Don't wait like I did.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turned Lena from cutting to building: she'd start the jam stall straight away. Her advice to her husband came from her own regret about waiting too long at the supermarket. She watches neighbouring farms' packing lines as her warning sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68, so that one's mostly about Imran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, ten years is plenty to get people ready, so there's no excuse. Maybe I'd say we should be careful not to rush it, either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, I'd be retired. For Imran it's a problem, he'd be 63, three years short. So it's my worry, just through him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Millbrook as long as my back holds, keep the jam going, keep saving. I'd want Imran to start looking at other work in a few years, once we see which way things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for him more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good about this picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get better at pruning before I retire, I suppose. Rosa might finally stop redoing my trees. And I'd see the grandchildren grow up without the fear that it all lands at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and something with your head, both. I only ever had the hands, and the hands are what the robots go after now.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to get people ready, so there's no excuse, but we shouldn't rush it either.
S4.think: It's fine for me because I'd be retired, but my husband would be three years short of his pension. So it's my worry, through him.
S4.do: Keeps working at the farm while her back holds, keeps the jam stall going and keeps saving. Plans for her husband to look at other work in a few years once the direction is clear.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for her husband than herself.
S4.quote: I only ever had the hands, and the hands are what the robots go after now.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years shifts Lena's worry entirely onto her younger husband. She saw small good things, like more time to get better at pruning. Her advice to grandchildren was to learn both hands and head work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits me and Imran at the same time. What would help is some money for couples who both lose work in the same year, enough to keep the rent paid, and help for older people to get to their pension without losing the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the husbands and wives. Everyone thinks about one job. In our house there's two, and they could both go the same way.

headlineQuote: Mr Hale lets us take the cracked eggs home, which helps more than you'd think. I make a lot of omelettes.
portrait: Lena Khan is 58 and works at Millbrook, a farm with three thousand hens, an apple orchard and hay, where she packs eggs and prunes trees badly enough that a colleague redoes them. She spent twenty-five years at a supermarket until self-checkouts cut her hours, and she's learned to watch for lost hours rather than sackings. She and her husband Imran, a 53-year-old van driver, live paycheck to paycheck, and his job is as exposed as hers. She's pragmatic, uses AI on her phone now and then, and plans a jam stall from orchard windfalls. Fast AGI frightens her because it could take both incomes in one year, while ten years mostly worries her for Imran.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it could take her farm job and her husband's van job in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: Money for couples who both lose work at once, enough to keep paying rent, and help for older workers to reach their pension without losing their home.
